new_statements.rule_in_words: Changsha Xiang is a six-tone language; in ordinary disyllabic (prosodic) words the first syllable is metrically strong (trochaic / left-dominant): it is longer (mean ratio 1.53:1) and keeps its citation tone, while the second syllable is shortened and its tone levelled to a sandhi (near-neutral) tone. A right-dominant (final-strong) pattern with sandhi on the first syllable occurs in a restricted set of structures (per Lin 2011 and Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026: subject-predicate, verb-object, verb-resultative phrases and proper names).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Changsha; Zhong 2007 (abstract) proposes a multi-level metrical structure (syllable, foot, colon, prosodic word) in which some stress-level distinctions are not phonetically realised.
new_statements.exceptions: Right-dominant (final-prominent) structures limited to 'a few grammatical categories' (Guo & Chen); per Lin 2011 abstract and Zhang et al. 2026 slides these are subject-predicate, verb-object, verb-result constructions and proper names; trisyllabic sandhi directionality is not morphosyntactically governed (Lin 2011). Young speakers merge T13/T24 (Zhang et al.).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns disyllabic prosodic words (lexical compounds) produced in a carrier sentence; prominence is diagnosed via tone-sandhi dominance, duration and contour preservation rather than via an independent stress phoneme. Phrase-level prominence (V-O etc.) patterns differently (right-dominant).
new_statements.identity_note: All stress statements found concern the Changsha (長沙) city dialect, the standard representative of New Xiang (Glottolog xian1251 > Chang-Yi subgroup, Changsha; ISO hsn). Peng 2022 (also examined) describes Cenchuan in Pingjiang county, a Gan/Xiang transitional variety, and says nothing about word stress beyond listing qingsheng (toneless) particles/suffixes. Guo & Chen 2022 explicitly restrict their Changsha claim to left-dominant disyllabic prosodic words and note that a right-dominant pattern exists for a few grammatical structures (verb-object, subject-predicate, verb-resultative, proper names per Lin 2011 / Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026).

sources.note: Instrumental study (5 Changsha speakers, 180 disyllables): Changsha Xiang disyllabic prosodic words are left-dominant / strong-weak: sigma1 is metrically strong, longer (ratio 1.53:1) and keeps its citation tone, sigma2 is reduced to a level sandhi tone; a right-dominant pattern (sandhi on sigma1) exists but 'is only limited to a few grammatical categories' (pp. 3, 5, 14-15).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Slides (not a publication) summarising Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026 J. Phonetics: Changsha has structure-dependent tone sandhi, left-in the dominant set modifier-head/coordinative words, right-in the dominant set subject-predicate, verb-object, verb-result and proper names (after Lin 2011); dominant syllables ~100 ms longer with fuller tonal contrasts; authors argue sandhi 'may reflect metrical prominence (stress) at the word level' but 'more research.. is needed to establish stress in Changsha Xiang'.
